title: StatsMonitor
oneLiner: A daily reliability pipeline for 13 robot controllers at 6 customer sites: raw telemetry in, a ranked watchlist out for the service team. I built it alone, about 5,800 lines of Python with daily and weekly views, and it was running unattended at handoff.
cardSummary: Daily Python pipeline that ranks fleet robot controllers by reliability risk
metaDescription: I built StatsMonitor alone at Mujin: a daily Python pipeline that ranks 13 robot controllers at 6 customer sites by reliability risk for the service team.
whatIOwnedSummary: All of it: telemetry ingestion, the layered data store, the KPI definitions, coverage tracking and evidence gates, the risk score and watchlist, the daily report and its analysis panel, and the operating guide the service team adopted. Internal details are left out of this page.

claims.title: Worked with a service teammate to trace a customer's throughput drop to a packaging defect, then wrote the operating guide
claims.ownedScope: A customer opened a support case about throughput at one controller. I worked the telemetry side of a joint investigation with a service teammate, using the report I'd built, then wrote the operating guide the service team adopted for future cases.
claims.method:
In the report's analysis panel, I compared the controller's picks per hour, error-induced downtime share, and human interventions per 10k picks from the week of the case with a window a month earlier, when it had no complaints. I didn't compare across the fleet, because sites handle different materials and direct cross-site comparisons aren't reliable.
Once the metrics showed it getting worse, I went through camera footage from that site and period. It showed the gripper tearing the tops of boxes that had a hole in the top face.
claims.resultMetric: The cause was a packaging defect. A hole in the top face of incoming boxes broke the vacuum seal, so the gripper tore the box tops on pick attempts. The findings went to my manager and the service team, and the operating guide came out of this work.
claims.limitations: The KPI tables are daily, so we couldn't narrow the failure to hours or shifts. The footage check was a separate manual step, since the pipeline doesn't pull in video. The service team handled the conversation with the customer, so fixing the packaging was downstream of my work, and I don't know whether the customer changed its packaging spec.

claims.title: Replaced a one-number ranking with a score that shows which controller is worst, and why
claims.ownedScope: The old ranking used one metric, error-induced downtime per 10k picks. I decided to replace it with a score that combines three reliability signals, normalizes them across the active controllers, and names each flagged controller's dominant driver. Controllers were usually falling short for different reasons, so the service team needed to see which was worst against its peers, and why, and start there instead of guessing.
claims.method: The inputs are three rates per 10k picks: error-pause time, pick errors, and human interventions. Each is min-max normalized across the eligible controllers in the current 7-day window, then weighted. I started near an even split and shifted weight toward the metrics that best signaled a real need for service, so error-pause time weighs most and human interventions least. The driver is the largest normalized component before weighting, so it names the metric most extreme against peers, not the one adding most to the score. It maps to a watchlist category: error-induced downtime, pick errors, or human interventions. Only controllers with at least 5 days with required stats, 3 days with picks, and 15,000 picks in the window get scored.
claims.resultMetric: The watchlist puts the worst controller first. Each row shows how severe it is (color), what triggered it (driver category), and what to check (the operating guide's recommended action). Because the score is relative to peers, the team doesn't have to compare absolute thresholds across controllers running in different conditions.
claims.limitations: Because the score is relative to peers, it will rank a fleet that's all performing about the same, but the absolute risk level stays unclear. It also can't tell a bad reading from a real change. When numbers didn't add up, the pipeline flagged them for a person to check, but the score would have ranked them like any other. The weights were tuned for this fleet's failure patterns and would likely need re-tuning for a fleet that fails differently.

claims.title: Built week-over-week trend detection that flags worsening controllers without low-volume false alerts
claims.ownedScope: The risk score says which controller is worst, not which way it's heading. The team would want to treat a controller holding steady at high severity differently from one getting worse each week. So I built a trend layer that compares each controller's current 7-day window with the prior one on four metrics, labels each worsening, rising, improving, or stable, and rolls them into one badge. Per-metric noise floors keep low-volume controllers from raising false alerts.
claims.method: The metrics are error-pause time, pick errors, human interventions, and downtime share, compared across two non-overlapping weeks. The badge takes the worst active signal, and it leans toward escalation. Worsening triggers above a 25% increase and rising at 10%, but a metric only counts as improving after a drop of more than 25%, and the badge only says improving if every active metric is moving the right way. One stable metric is enough to keep it from saying improving. The intent is to flag decline quickly and call recovery slowly. I set the noise floors from first principles. A metric where both weeks are under its floor sits out the vote, since a percentage change on a near-zero baseline isn't a meaningful signal. If either week breaks the floor, it stays in, so a real jump from quiet to loud still counts. The prior week also has to pass a coverage check. A gap last week means no badge this week, even if this week is clean.
claims.resultMetric: At handoff, the watchlist showed two signals per controller, severity (how bad it is now) and trajectory (whether it's getting worse), and the service team used both together. A "Degrading yellow" controller can come before a "stable red" one, because its problem is still unfolding. The badge feeds the same escalation paths in the operating guide as the severity color, so a controller that stays Degrading triggers an escalation step.
claims.limitations: The trend logic assumes higher is worse, which holds for all four metrics. A future metric where higher is better, like throughput or uptime, would be mislabeled unless the classifier's sign were flipped. It also can't tell a real performance change from a known operational one, like a customer adding a new SKU or running a different shift pattern. The team has to bring that context.

claims.title: Built the pipeline to flag missing or thin data instead of guessing
claims.ownedScope: I built the pipeline around one rule, written down in the project as "missing data is not zero, always consider coverage." Thin data isn't confirmed data either. A controller that reported no telemetry for a day shouldn't produce a healthy-looking "zero events, zero downtime" picture, and one with too little activity shouldn't have conclusions drawn from it. I built coverage tracking and evidence gates in from the start.
claims.method: For each controller and day, the pipeline records which raw stats arrived from the upstream feed, separate from what they parsed to. That's how you tell a 0 that means the robot was idle from a 0 that means nothing was reported. A controller that fails any of the three evidence gates (days with required stats, days with picks, total picks) gets no performance row and stays out of the peer ranking, instead of being misranked against fully covered peers. If it's short on days with required stats, it gets a missing-data row, red if telemetry went fully dark and yellow if partial. That row points at data and infrastructure, so the team knows to check the connection, the stats export, and the pipeline schedule, not the hardware. Rates use only the days that reported, so a 5-day rate isn't scaled up to look like a 7-day one.
claims.resultMetric: Each card shows the service team two separate signals. Severity (color and category) says whether the controller is unhealthy. Coverage says whether its data can be trusted: green and red squares for which of the last 7 days had required stats, with a count below. Unreliable data gets its own watchlist row, pointed at the team that should check it, instead of passing as a performance signal. Time-breakdown bars and trend tables leave blanks, not zeros, where data is missing.
claims.limitations: Data quality is pass-fail per day, though some stats can arrive partially. I gave up that nuance because the service team reads a pass-fail view, not a confidence score. The evidence gates are tuned to this fleet's reporting cadence and would likely need adjusting for another. They also check whether stats arrived, not whether they're right. Readings that didn't add up went to a person to check instead of being rejected automatically.

claims.title: Built the nightly pipeline to run unattended, then hardened it against failures seen in production
claims.ownedScope: It ran every night on a production server with nobody watching, pulling real telemetry from a deployed fleet. I designed it around hard timeouts on every network call, stepped backoff for controllers that fail, no external pip dependencies, and a layered bronze/silver/gold data store. Some of that was right in the first version. The rest I revised after production failures showed me where I was wrong.
claims.method:
Three layers keep it from hanging. The telemetry API call has a SIGALRM hard timeout that raises into the per-controller retry loop. Each controller connection has socket-level connect timeouts and a poll loop with a deadline. The whole job runs under a Bash timeout in the cron entry, so no single layer can hang the run. I built it this way after early trouble automating the per-controller connections, which either failed silently or took too long to come up.

The backfill runner backs off a failing controller in steps: 15 minutes after the first failure, 1 hour after the second, 6 hours after the third, 24 hours after the fourth. The state lives in a JSON file, so a controller that failed yesterday is still cooling down today. A controller can be unreachable for days, and without backoff it would be retried on every run.

The core code has no external pip dependencies and no requirements.txt or pyproject.toml. The only outside code is the vendored API client, included as a git submodule. I chose that to keep deployment simple, limit dependency drift, and keep the pipeline small enough for me to understand and own all of it.

Bronze (raw merged JSON per controller per day) is the canonical store, and silver (flattened CSVs) and gold (aggregated KPIs, the watchlist, the HTML report) are built from it. It lives on the pipeline server, not with the controllers, by design from the start, so the full history is in one place the pipeline owns and silver and gold can be rebuilt at any time.
claims.resultMetric: At handoff, it ran nightly without intervention. A controller that can't be reached or returns an error is logged to a failure CSV, and the rest of the run finishes. Partial failures no longer quietly advance the state and leave gaps in the history.
claims.limitations: An early version of the backfill runner advanced its cursor on partial failures, which left silent gaps in the archive. That bug shipped. I caught it in production while tracking down why some days were missing telemetry, and fixed it by refusing to advance the cursor on a partial failure and queuing those windows for retry.

claims.title: Built a side-by-side analysis panel with 15 months of controller history
claims.ownedScope: The watchlist says which controllers to look at. The analysis panel, which I designed and built at the top of the daily report, is what lets the service team investigate, comparing two controllers side by side or following one over time.
claims.method:
You pick two controllers, optionally a date range, and toggle three KPIs: picks per hour, error-induced downtime share, and human interventions per 10k picks. Each controller gets its own chart, because three KPIs is already six lines and overlaying a second controller would make twelve. Separate charts stay readable and leave room for more KPIs.

The charts share a Y-axis maximum, so one controller's spike isn't rescaled just because the other is mostly flat, and magnitudes compare directly. Hover is synced across both. I added that after the first version, since reading one chart at a time defeated the point of side by side.

The charts show daily data, with a weekly toggle for trends over a few weeks, and switch to monthly on their own past about 90 days, where daily lines are unreadable and the team rarely needs day-level detail. Rates come from bucket totals (sum of picks over sum of active hours), not averages of daily rates, which bias the result.

Days that failed the required-stats check show as dashed, faded gaps in the daily charts, not smoothed-over lines. It's the same coverage gating the rest of the pipeline uses.

It's about 1,000 lines of vanilla JavaScript on Chart.js, which I chose because it's light, needs no build step, and works in a single-file HTML report opened locally. No framework, no bundler, no build pipeline.
claims.resultMetric: The service team used the side-by-side view to compare two gripper systems directly. I also used the panel in a separate project, during end-of-arm tooling (EOAT) validation testing, to compare the incumbent vacuum cup with its replacement under field conditions over multiple weeks. Two metrics from that test plan became standard StatsMonitor outputs.
claims.limitations: It suits the small fleet it was built for, a curated set of controllers chosen for active deployment and accessible telemetry. A few are left out of the dropdowns for known data-quality or telemetry-access reasons. Comparison is pairwise only, and a bigger fleet would need a rethought dropdown, probably with grouping or filtering. Past 90 days, monthly buckets drop day-level detail entirely, so finding one day from months back means narrowing the range by hand.

claims.title: Wrote the watchlist's operating guide, which the service team adopted
claims.ownedScope: The service team, not engineers, would use the report day to day, and they needed to know what each flag means, what to do about it, and when to escalate. I wrote the guide as part of my handoff, so the diagnostic process would be on paper when I left, not just in the code.
claims.method:
Seven sections: what the watchlist is, how severity is set, what each category means and what to check, reading trend badges, reading a card step by step, using the analysis panel, and escalation paths. A quick reference lists the key thresholds, so the team can see why a controller is flagged.

Section 5, "Reading a Watchlist Card," is six steps: check severity and the trend badge, read the trigger reason, read the recommended action, check the owner field for which team handles the category, review the evidence to collect before closing or escalating, and use the visualizations for context. The idea was a set procedure, so nobody on the service team has to interpret the report on their own.

The escalation paths send each kind of persistent flag to the team that handles it. Persistent red goes to the controls team, for example, and persistent missing data to data and infrastructure. The report flags the problem, and the guide routes the response.

The company's senior technical writer reviewed the draft, suggested a few formatting changes, and signed off. I made the changes and finalized it.
claims.resultMetric: The service team adopted the guide. A coworker mentioned wanting to put the report up on an office monitor so the team could see all the controllers at once. I handed the guide and the codebase to a coworker before my last day.
claims.limitations: The writer's review was fairly light and focused on formatting, not a deep content review. When I left, the guide hadn't been tried on enough real cases to know whether its actions and escalation paths cover everything the team will run into. The quick-reference thresholds are tuned for this fleet and would need updating if the fleet or its operating conditions change much. It also assumes the reader already knows the warehouse robot system's basic vocabulary.

outcome: Running nightly and unattended at handoff. The service team adopted the watchlist and its operating guide, and the report's analysis panel helped diagnose a customer's throughput drop as a packaging defect. Before my last day, I handed the pipeline and the guide to a coworker and confirmed it was running on their end.

interfaces.notes: Per-controller, per-day pulls of several stat types through a vendored API client, merged into one JSON file per controller-day with a generatedAt timestamp. Failures go to a per-stat failure CSV and the run continues.

Incremental flatten to one row per (controller, day, stat). A state file limits re-flattening to changed or re-pulled files. Coverage is kept in a separate ledger, so missing data stays distinct from zero-event days.

Daily KPIs per controller-day: picks per hour, error-induced downtime share, interventions per 10k picks, and pick-outcome and error-category distributions. Risk score and week-over-week trends over 7-day windows, behind the evidence gates. Missing data is its own watchlist category. Debug tables sit beside the watchlist for tracing results back.
Static HTML report with the analysis panel, rebuilt daily from the gold tables. The renderer writes to a known path, and the team added hosting on top with no code changes.
Turns the system's outputs into a playbook: severity actions, category checks, trend badges, escalation paths to specific teams, and key thresholds. The service team adopted it during my handoff.

projectRisks: The pipeline depends on the upstream telemetry API staying stable. There are no contract tests to catch a schema change before it breaks a daily run.
Score weights, evidence gates, and noise floors are tuned to this fleet's failure patterns. They don't adjust on their own as the fleet grows or the customer mix changes.

lessons.text: When several controllers are each falling short for a different reason, one metric can't tell you which is worst. A combined score that names its driver works better.
A report that drives decisions has to show how good its data is. A zero that could mean "no events" or "no data" will mislead whoever reads it.

Reliability came from iteration as much as upfront design. Several of the pipeline's most important reliability features came from patching real failures in production, not from getting everything right the first time.
